title.narrative: WGG- Research and Documentation in Rwanda

description.narrative: The strategy of research and documentation is integral to the learning and evidence building agenda of the WGG Consortium and its country-level strategic partners. There are significant programmatic components of the consortium wide joint activities as part of global and regional advocacy efforts.

sector.narrative: Support for feminist, women-led and women's rights organisations and movements, and institutions (governmental and non-govermental) at all levels to enhance their effectiveness, influence and substainability (activities and core-funding). These organisations exist to bring about transformative change for gender equality and/or the rights of women and girls in developing countries. Their activities include agenda-setting, advocacy, policy dialogue, capacity development, awareness raising and prevention, service provision, conflict-prevention and peacebuilding, research, organising, and alliance and network building

Adolescent Girls Leadership Academy in RwandaThe 5-day workshop was attended by 20 adolescent girls who participated actively facilitated by feminists from Rwanda and Kenya. The academy built the capacity of the adolescent girls on leadership, self-esteem and personal identity, decision-making, gender, and GBV. They then developed action plans to establish girls clubs in schools in their region.AFRO ARKTraining of 30 adolescent girls including girls with disability on women rights, SRHR and SGBV in NyagatareNumber of people: 30 girls and girls with disabilities (15 girls and 15 GWD)Impact: Girls and Girls with Disabilities engage policymakers, program planners, and their families and communities join them as they lead efforts to access their rights, especially in relation to their sexual and reproductive health and protection from GBV perpetrated against them.Afro Ark mapped 50 adolescent girls and put them in 2 cohorts. This year was an electioneering year in Rwanda, which caused a delay in executing some of the activities and heightened government surveillance was an evident risk. From a safeguarding standpoint, we had to pivot from conducting actual political scorecards, opting to train young women on conducting political scorecards, and had 50 young women participants. Through neutral framing and training approach, participants were trained on scorecard methodologies and equipped with skills relevant to governance processes such as public participation and local accountability.
